title: Why doesn't knowing help?
hookLine: a king who has lost everything and a merchant thrown out by his own family meet in a forest, and neither can stop worrying
carry: the goddess who binds the mind, and frees it
tomorrow: The goddess who is Vishnu's sleep

lines: A KING RIDES INTO A FOREST ALONE.
cards: A king rides into a forest alone, his kingdom lost. Enemies beat him in battle, then his own ministers turned on him and took the treasury. He finds the quiet hermitage of a sage named Medhas, and stays.
And under the trees he can't stop worrying. Is my elephant fed? Are my servants treated well?
Is my treasure being wasted? Then he meets a merchant named Samadhi, sitting there just as lost. That's how the Devi Mahatmya begins, and year four reads it whole.

teach.b: Devi Mahatmya means the glory of the goddess. Tradition places it inside the Markandeya Purana; it's also called the Chandi, and some homes and temples recite it whole. Yet it opens with no goddess at all.
The merchant's is the harder one. His own wife and sons, greedy for his money, threw him out. And still he can't stop wondering whether they're well.
So they bring the sage one honest question. In paraphrase: we know these things have left us. So why do we still grieve?
Why doesn't knowing help? Medhas doesn't call them foolish. He points at birds: hungry themselves, they still drop grain into the beaks of their young.

Every creature, he says, is pulled this way. Then he names the pull: Mahamaya, the great illusion, and in this text she is the goddess herself. She seizes the minds of even the wise and drags them into confusion.
And the same goddess, when gracious, sets people free. That's the surprise, and the teaching.

teach.h: SHAKTI: THE POWER BEHIND IT ALL.
teach.b: For Shakta Hindus, who worship the goddess as supreme, she is Shakti, the power behind everything: even the pull these men carried into the forest, and the freedom from it.
That's why her devotees pray to her for release, not only for help.
The king asks: who is this goddess? Medhas answers with stories, and the rest of the book is those stories.

how: Some Hindus recite the Devi Mahatmya, also called the Chandi or Durga Saptashati, from beginning to end, especially during Navaratri, and it is recited in some temples devoted to the goddess.

o: a guide to temple rites for the goddess's priests
a king's diary of the battles that cost his throne
the glory of the goddess, a book of her stories

s: the Devi Mahatmya opens with the goddess in battle
it opens with a king and a merchant in a forest, asking a sage why they still grieve.
the merchant still worries about the family that threw him out
he can't stop wondering whether they're well.
in the text, the goddess who binds minds is also the one who frees them
Medhas says Mahamaya seizes even the wise, and, when gracious, sets people free.

games.q: you're the merchant. your family threw you out for your money. a sage asks what's on your mind. what is it?
o: how to get the money back.
whether my wife and sons are well.
games.why: he keeps wondering whether they're well. that's his question for the sage: why does my mind go back to people who sent me away?

practice: Let one thing your mind keeps going back to come up on its own, a person, a place, something gone that still pulls, and notice the pull the way the merchant noticed his, without arguing or fixing.
With each breath out, let the grip loosen a little; if you pray, hold it before God or the goddess in your own words, and if you don't, let the breath do the holding.
If that pull is ever too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
